q: In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, the catalyst used is:
x: Ammonia is made over finely divided iron promoted with small amounts of K₂O and Al₂O₃. V₂O₅ is the contact process catalyst and platinum gauze is used in the Ostwald process, so those are the usual mix-ups.

q: Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory: 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O. What volume of ammonia at STP is obtained from 10.7 g of NH₄Cl? (N = 14, H = 1, Cl = 35.5; molar volume 22.4 dm³)
x: M(NH₄Cl) = 53.5 g mol⁻¹, so 10.7 g = 0.20 mol; NH₄Cl and NH₃ are 2 : 2, so 0.20 mol NH₃ = 0.20 × 22.4 = 4.48 dm³. Halving the moles as if 2 mol NH₄Cl gave 1 mol NH₃ gives 2.24 dm³.

q: A sealed tube of brown nitrogen dioxide becomes much paler when it is placed in ice. This is because:
o: 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ is exothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium towards colourless N₂O₄
NO₂ condenses to a colourless liquid on cooling
NO₂ decomposes into colourless N₂ and O₂ on cooling
Cooling shifts 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄ towards brown NO₂
x: The dimerisation of brown NO₂ into colourless N₂O₄ releases heat, so lowering the temperature favours N₂O₄ and the colour fades. Reversing the direction of the shift is the usual Le Chatelier slip.

q: Colourless concentrated nitric acid turns yellow when it stands in light for some time. The yellow colour is due to:
o: Dissolved NO₂ formed by the decomposition 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O
Dissolved N₂O formed by the decomposition of the acid
Iron impurities dissolved from the bottle
Ammonium nitrate formed by reduction of the acid
x: Light decomposes nitric acid into NO₂, O₂ and water, and the brown NO₂ dissolving in the acid gives a yellow colour; that is why it is kept in brown bottles. N₂O is colourless, so it cannot cause the colour.

q: 6.35 g of copper reacts completely with hot concentrated nitric acid. What volume of gas, measured at STP, is given off? (Cu = 63.5; molar volume 22.4 dm³)
x: Concentrated acid gives NO₂: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O. 0.10 mol Cu gives 0.20 mol NO₂ = 4.48 dm³. Using the dilute-acid equation (2 mol NO per 3 mol Cu) gives 1.49 dm³, the most tempting wrong answer.

q: Iron dissolves in dilute nitric acid, but after being dipped in concentrated nitric acid it no longer reacts with dilute acid. This is because concentrated HNO₃:
o: Forms a thin, protective oxide layer on the iron, making it passive
Reduces the iron surface to a more stable form
Deposits a layer of iron(II) nitrate that will not dissolve
Converts the iron into an alloy with nitrogen
x: Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and coats iron (also Al and Cr) with a thin, unreactive oxide film; this is called passivity. Nitrates of iron are soluble in water, so a nitrate layer could not protect the metal.

q: In waterlogged soil, some bacteria convert nitrate ions into nitrogen gas, which returns to the atmosphere. This step of the nitrogen cycle is called:
x: Denitrifying bacteria in oxygen-poor soil reduce NO₃⁻ to N₂. Nitrification is the opposite direction (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), and fixation turns N₂ into compounds, so nitrification is the tempting mix-up.

q: White phosphorus is converted into red phosphorus by:
o: Burning it in a limited supply of air
Heating it to about 250 °C in the absence of air
Dissolving it in carbon disulphide and evaporating the solvent
Boiling it with sodium hydroxide solution
x: Heating white phosphorus at about 250 °C out of contact with air links the P₄ units into polymeric red phosphorus. Burning gives oxides, CS₂ only recrystallises white phosphorus, and NaOH gives phosphine.

q: Phosphorus pentachloride is treated with a limited amount of water. The products are:
x: Partial hydrolysis replaces two Cl atoms by one O: PCl₅ + H₂O → POCl₃ + 2HCl. H₃PO₄ forms only with excess water, so it is the tempting answer if the word limited is ignored; H₃PO₃ comes from PCl₃, not PCl₅.

q: In the P₄O₁₀ molecule, each P atom is bonded to four O atoms, and the P atoms are linked through P–O–P bridges. How many oxygen atoms are in P–O–P bridges?
x: P₄O₁₀ is the P₄O₆ cage (six bridging O along the six edges of the P₄ tetrahedron) plus one terminal P=O on each of the four P atoms: 6 + 4 = 10 O. Check: each P has 3 bridging + 1 terminal = 4 O. Giving the 4 terminal oxygens is the slip.

q: Orthophosphoric acid heated strongly loses water to give metaphosphoric acid: H₃PO₄ → HPO₃ + H₂O. The oxidation state of phosphorus and the basicity of HPO₃ are:
x: In HPO₃: +1 + x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +5 (unchanged, since losing water is not redox); it has one O–H group, so it is monobasic. Keeping the basicity of the parent H₃PO₄ gives +5 and 3.

q: White phosphorus is warmed with NaOH solution: P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂. This reaction is best described as, with the oxidation states of phosphorus formed:
x: Phosphorus starts at 0; in PH₃ it is −3 and in H₂PO₂⁻ it is +1 (2(+1) + x + 2(−2) = −1). One element is both reduced and oxidised, so it is disproportionation; electron check: 1 P gains 3 e⁻ while 3 P lose 1 e⁻ each. Assuming the oxyanion is phosphite (+3) is the tempting slip.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes red phosphorus from white phosphorus?
o: Red phosphorus glows in the dark in moist air, whereas white phosphorus does not
Red phosphorus is insoluble in carbon disulphide, whereas white phosphorus dissolves in it
Red phosphorus consists of discrete P₄ molecules, whereas white phosphorus is polymeric
Red phosphorus is highly poisonous, whereas white phosphorus is not
x: Polymeric red phosphorus does not dissolve in CS₂, while molecular P₄ (white) does. The other statements are all reversed: white phosphorus glows, is molecular and is very poisonous.

q: In the laboratory, phosphorus pentoxide (P₄O₁₀) is used mainly as:
o: A powerful drying and dehydrating agent
x: P₄O₁₀ combines very strongly with water to form phosphoric acids, so it is used to dry gases and to dehydrate compounds. Phosphorus is already in its highest (+5) state in it, so it cannot act as a reducing agent.

q: Plastic (amorphous) sulphur is obtained by:
o: Cooling a solution of sulphur in carbon disulphide slowly
Melting rhombic sulphur and letting it cool slowly in a crucible
Pouring nearly boiling sulphur into cold water
x: Sudden cooling of hot, viscous sulphur (long chains) in cold water traps the chains and gives rubbery plastic sulphur. Slow crystallisation from CS₂ gives rhombic sulphur and slow cooling of the melt gives monoclinic needles.

q: In the contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (ΔH negative) is run at about 450 °C rather than at a much lower temperature because:
o: Higher temperatures increase the equilibrium yield of SO₃
Lower temperatures give a higher yield but the reaction becomes too slow, so 450 °C is a compromise
x: The forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature favours SO₃ at equilibrium, but the rate becomes too slow even with V₂O₅; 450 °C gives a good yield at a useful rate. Thinking a higher temperature raises the yield ignores the sign of ΔH.

q: Hot concentrated sulphuric acid reacts with charcoal. The products are:
x: Hot concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as an oxidising agent: C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2SO₂ + 2H₂O, carbon going from 0 to +4 and sulphur from +6 to +4. Electron check: C loses 4 e⁻ and two S gain 2 e⁻ each. H₂S forms only with strong reducing agents, not carbon.

q: Oleum, H₂S₂O₇, is diluted with water: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. What mass of H₂SO₄ is obtained from 17.8 g of oleum? (H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)
x: M(H₂S₂O₇) = 2 + 64 + 112 = 178 g mol⁻¹, so 0.10 mol gives 0.20 mol H₂SO₄ = 0.20 × 98 = 19.6 g. Mass check: 17.8 g oleum + 1.8 g water = 19.6 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 9.8 g.

q: Concentrated sulphuric acid is a good drying agent, but it is NOT suitable for drying:
x: Ammonia is a base and reacts with the acid to form ammonium sulphate, so it is absorbed instead of dried. Cl₂, CO₂ and SO₂ are acidic or neutral and do not react, so they can be dried by passing through concentrated H₂SO₄.

q: Sulphur dioxide is bubbled through acidified potassium dichromate solution. The colour change and the role of SO₂ are:
o: Green to orange; SO₂ is an oxidising agent
Orange to colourless; SO₂ is a bleaching agent only
Orange to yellow; SO₂ is a base
Orange to green; SO₂ is a reducing agent
x: SO₂ (S +4) is oxidised to sulphate (+6) and reduces orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ (Cr +6) to green Cr³⁺. Reversing the colours treats SO₂ as the oxidant, the usual slip.

q: What volume of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NaOH is needed to neutralise 25 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ completely to Na₂SO₄?
x: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Acid = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol, so NaOH = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol, and 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.10 = 0.050 dm³ = 50 cm³. Treating sulphuric acid as monobasic gives 25 cm³.
